novel_idea.topic_thesis: Agentic Slop begins when organizations count plausible AI artifacts as throughput before those artifacts reach a boundary of consequence.
novel_idea.angle: Diagnose the organization where agents generate drafts, analyses, tickets, campaigns, and code faster than anyone can test, own, reject, or delete them. The failure is not poor model quality; it is mistaking work in process for value. The operator move is to cap agency work in process and require doctrine, ownership, kill criteria, and reality feedback before increasing generation.
novel_idea.hook: If your agents keep producing while your operators keep cleaning, you are not scaling throughput. You are scaling Agentic Slop.
novel_idea.argument_summary: AI makes plausible artifacts cheap, but an artifact remains organizational inventory until it reaches a boundary where customers, operations, markets, or other consequences can answer. Without that reality contact, every new output creates obligations to interpret, review, reconcile, supervise, and eventually delete. High-quality generation can therefore reduce useful throughput by consuming more coherence than it creates. This differs from the prior human-middleware argument: the problem is not primarily managers carrying context between machines or an unreformed org chart. It is the accounting error of treating generation as completed value. The corresponding operator decision is to limit agency work in process and refuse additional autonomous output unless each workflow has current doctrine, an owner, kill criteria, and a feedback path from consequence.
novel_idea.novelty_rationale: The closest post argues that retaining the old organizational architecture turns managers into context-carrying middleware between agents. This argument identifies a different failure mechanism that can persist even with direct doctrine-to-agent execution: generated artifacts are misclassified as throughput before reality has tested them. Its consequence is accumulating inventory and deletion burden, and its operator decision is to cap agency work in process rather than merely remove human relay nodes.
novel_idea.source_grounding: The source defines Agentic Slop as endless plausible output without taste, context, kill criteria, or deletion. The Coherence Ceiling chapter says each new channel creates obligations to interpret, supervise, review, handle exceptions, delete, and repair trust. The Actors chapter defines Actors as the boundary of consequence where doctrine meets reality and reality answers. The Goldratt letter distinguishes throughput from inventory and states that adding agency while the constraint remains flat raises inventory and operating expense rather than throughput. Appendix B explicitly recommends capping agency work in process and defining doctrine sources, owners, permissions, blast radii, evaluations, and feedback paths.

payload.body_text:
The pull request queue triples. Review capacity does not. Someone calls this productivity.

This is Agentic Slop: agents generate plausible work faster than the organization can test, own, reject, or delete it. The backlog looks like momentum. In reality, it is inventory piling up before a boundary of consequence.

The models are not the problem. The measurement is. Drafts, analyses, tickets, campaigns, and code are counted as throughput before they change a customer outcome, a production system, or a real decision.

Cap agency work in process. Require current doctrine, a named owner, kill criteria, and reality feedback before increasing generation.

Otherwise the company becomes a warehouse for plausible artifacts—and its best operators become full-time janitors.
